1.title: Heaven and Earth Are Called
1.context: Isaiah's book opens as a courtroom summons. The vision is dated by four kings of Judah, and its first witnesses are not people but heaven and earth themselves.
1.question: What does it change for you that God opens His case by calling witnesses instead of simply striking?

1.title: A Beaten Body, a Hut in a Field
1.context: The nation is pictured as one bruised body with no healthy spot, and Jerusalem as a lone hut left standing in a harvested field. Only a remnant's survival keeps the city from Sodom's total end.
1.question: Where in your own life has God left a small standing remnant when everything else fell?

1.title: What Are Your Sacrifices to Me?
1.context: God addresses worshipers in Sodom and Gomorrah's names while their hands are full of offerings. The shock is deliberate: ritual kept, hands bloody, prayers unheard.
1.question: What religious habit might God be calling empty in your life right now?

1.title: Wash, and Reason Together
1.context: The remedy is a bath and a school: stop the evil, learn to do right, seek justice. Then comes the famous invitation to reason together, with scarlet sins promised white as snow.
1.question: Which of the chapter's commands, wash, learn, seek justice, resist the oppressor, is the one you most avoid?

1.title: The Faithful City
1.context: The chapter ends with the city renamed by its conduct, once faithful, now a prostitute, its silver turned to dross. But Zion will be redeemed with justice, and the rebels' end is pictured as an unquenchable fire.
1.question: What would your own city or church be renamed by its conduct?

2.title: The Mountain Above the Mountains
2.context: Chapter two shows the destination before the disaster: nations streaming up God's mountain, weapons refitted as farm tools, and an invitation to walk in the light now.
2.question: What would it look like to beat one of your own swords into a plowshare this week?

2.title: Full of Everything but Trust
2.context: Judah's land is full of silver, horses, and idols, everything except trust. Against all of it stands one day, the day of the LORD, before which the lofty are brought low.
2.question: Which fullness in your life most competes with trust in God?

2.title: The Supply Removed
2.context: Judgment here is administrative: God removes bread, water, soldiers, judges, and prophets, and society collapses into children ruling and neighbors oppressing neighbors.
2.question: What props hold your own world up, and what would remain if God removed them?

2.title: The Daughters of Zion
2.context: The finery of Jerusalem's proud women is inventoried piece by piece and then stripped away. The parade through the chapter is the book's portrait of a society admiring itself on the edge of ruin.
2.question: What finery does your own generation parade that this passage would inventory?

2.title: The Branch and the Canopy
2.context: Six verses answer the stripping: a Branch who is beautiful and glorious, a washed remnant called holy, and God's glory spread over Zion like a wedding canopy.
2.question: Where do you need God to be a canopy, shade by day and shelter in the storm, right now?

3.title: The Song of the Vineyard
3.context: The book's third sound is a love song sung by a friend for his vineyard, dug, cleared, planted with choice vines. The question it leaves hanging is the owner's: what more could have been done?
3.question: When you look at what God has done for you, what is your honest answer to His question?

3.title: The Hedge Taken Away
3.context: The sentence is the removal of protection, and the verdict names the crop: God looked for justice and saw bloodshed, for righteousness and heard a cry of distress. The vineyard is the house of Israel.
3.question: What hedge of God's protection have you treated as permanent that this song says can be removed?

3.title: Woe to the Land Grabbers and the Drinkers
3.context: The first woes fall on economics and anesthesia: houses joined to houses until one family owns the view, and strong drink chased from morning until the harp drowns out God's work.
3.question: Which of these two woes, accumulation or escape, stands closer to your own door?

3.title: Dragging Sin by Cords
3.context: The remaining woes go inward: sin hauled like a cart, evil called good and good evil, men wise in their own eyes and heroes at mixing drinks while justice is sold for a bribe.
3.question: Where have you quietly renamed something God calls evil with a softer name?

3.title: Fire and the Uplifted Hand
3.context: Fire answers the diagnosis, and the refrain first sounds that will toll through the book: for all this, His anger has not turned away; His hand is still upraised. A distant nation is already whistled for.
3.question: What does it mean to you that God's hand can be upraised and His invitation still standing in the same book?

4.title: In the Year Uzziah Died
4.context: Uzziah had reigned fifty-two years; his death is the date stamp on the book's commissioning vision. Isaiah sees the real King on the real throne, and his first word is woe on himself.
4.question: What loss or ending in your life has cleared your view of who is actually on the throne?

4.title: The Coal and the Sending
4.context: A seraph carries a coal in tongs to the prophet's condemned lips, and the cleansed man volunteers before he knows the assignment. The assignment is preaching to people who will not hear, until only a stump remains, and the stump is a holy seed.
4.question: Where is God sending you to speak faithfully without any promise that it will be received?

4.title: Shear-jashub at the Aqueduct
4.context: Syria and Israel march on Jerusalem, and God sends Isaiah with his son, whose name means a remnant will return, to tell the trembling king that two smoldering stubs of firewood will not prevail. Be careful, be quiet, do not fear.
4.question: What threat in your life looks like a fire and is, in God's accounting, only a smoldering stub?

4.title: The Sign of Immanuel
4.context: God offers King Ahaz any sign in heaven or Sheol; the king refuses with pious words, and God gives one anyway: a child called Immanuel, God with us, whose short childhood will measure how fast the threat collapses.
4.question: When have you refused to ask God for what He was offering to give?

5.title: Maher-shalal-hash-baz
5.context: The second placard child arrives by paperwork first: a large tablet, reliable witnesses, then a birth. Before the boy can say father or mother, the wealth of Damascus and Samaria will be carried off.
5.question: What is God writing large in your life right now that you would rather He wrote small?

5.title: The Flood Judah Chose
5.context: Judah refused the gentle waters of Shiloah and trusted Assyria instead, so the river Euphrates itself will flood up to the neck. Yet the flood's edge is named: the land is Immanuel's.
5.question: Where have you traded God's gentle supply for a stronger-looking rescue that became a flood?

5.title: The Stone in the Sanctuary
5.context: Isaiah is taught a discipline of fear: do not call conspiracy what the people call conspiracy. God Himself will be a sanctuary to some and a stone of stumbling to others, and the prophet seals the testimony among his disciples and waits.
5.question: Whose fears are you being pressured to adopt that God has told you not to fear?

5.title: Darkness, Then a Great Light
5.context: The chapter of darkness ends with the hungry cursing their king and their God, and then, with no transition, no more gloom: a great light, a child born, a government on His shoulders, of peace no end.
5.question: What darkness in your life most needs to hear that the light has already been announced over it?

5.title: The Bricks Have Fallen
5.context: Over Ephraim's pride the refrain tolls three times: we will rebuild with dressed stone, they say, while brother devours brother and the elders and prophets alike lead the people astray. His hand is still upraised.
5.question: Where are you rebuilding in pride exactly what God has been knocking down?

6.title: Woe to the Lawmakers
6.context: The movement's last refrain stroke falls on Judah's own courts: laws written to rob widows and orphans. When the day of reckoning comes, there will be no one to flee to and nowhere to leave the wealth.
6.question: What system do you benefit from that this woe would audit first?

6.title: The Axe Boasts Against the Woodsman
6.context: Assyria is the rod of God's anger, sent against a godless nation, but the rod has its own intentions and boasts as if it swung itself. God promises to punish the king's arrogant heart and burn his forests.
6.question: Where are you tempted to take credit for outcomes that God accomplished through you?

6.title: A Remnant Will Return
6.context: The forest arithmetic done, the promise turns: a remnant will return, not to the empire that struck them but to the Mighty God. Fear of Assyria is lifted, and the yoke will break because of the fatness, God's anointing.
6.question: What would it mean for you to rely on God instead of on the strongest thing that has hurt you?

6.title: The March on Jerusalem
6.context: The invasion is read town by town like a dispatch, Aiath, Migron, Nob, until the army shakes its fist at the mount of Daughter Zion. Then the forest falls again, and the tall trees are the empire's.
6.question: How do you pray when the threat can be tracked town by town and it is getting closer?

7.title: The Shoot of Jesse
7.context: Chapter six ended with a stump and chapter ten with a felled forest; chapter eleven grows one green shoot from Jesse's stump. The Spirit rests on Him in full, and He judges not by what His eyes see but with righteousness for the poor.
7.question: What felled stump in your life have you stopped expecting to sprout again?

7.title: The Wolf and the Lamb
7.context: The stump's orchard becomes the world's peace: predators lie down with prey, a child leads them, and the earth is full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.
7.question: Which pairing in your own world seems as impossible as wolf and lamb, and what does this picture ask you to hope?

7.title: His Hand a Second Time
7.context: The gathering is a second exodus: a remnant recovered from every compass point, the sea split again, a highway home from Assyria as there was from Egypt.
7.question: Where has God already brought you out once, and what would trusting Him for a second time look like?

7.title: The Song of the Delivered
7.context: Chapter twelve is six verses and is given whole, the song the delivered people will sing: anger turned away, salvation trusted without fear, water drawn with joy from the wells of salvation.
7.question: Which line of this short song could you make your own prayer today?

8.title: The Burden of Babylon
8.context: The burdens against the nations open with the empire that has not yet arrived. In Isaiah's lifetime Babylon is a province; the oracle already musters an army against her and darkens her stars.
8.question: How does it change your reading of today's powers that God addresses empires centuries before their peak?

8.title: The Jewel of Kingdoms, Fallen
8.context: Babylon's epitaph is written in Sodom's grammar: overthrown, uninhabited, given to wild animals. The Medes are already named as the instrument.
8.question: What Babylon of yours, impressive and permanent-looking, do you most need to hear is mortal?

8.title: How You Have Fallen, O Day Star
8.context: Israel's restoration frames a taunt: Sheol stirs its dead kings to greet Babylon's king, whose five boasts of I will end in maggots. The text aims the day star line at this king, in a song about his fall.
8.question: Which of the king's five I wills sounds most like the voice of your own ambition?

8.title: The Purpose That Stands
8.context: The horizon widens and narrows: Assyria crushed in God's own land, Philistia warned not to rejoice too soon, and over it all a purpose for the whole earth that no hand can reverse.
8.question: What decision of God are you currently trying to reverse, and what would resting under it look like?

9.title: My Heart Cries Out for Moab
9.context: The Moab burden is the strangest of the oracles because the prophet cannot stop grieving the nation he is sent to sentence. In one night Ar and Kir fall, and God's own heart cries out with the fugitives.
9.question: Who is God teaching you to grieve for, even while you cannot approve of where they stand?

9.title: Send the Lambs
9.context: Moab is counseled to send tribute lambs to Zion and shelter the fugitives, with a throne promised that will be established in loving devotion. The pride that refuses sets a three-year countdown instead.
9.question: What act of shelter or tribute is Moab's counsel asking of you toward God's people?

9.title: Damascus and Ephraim Together
9.context: The burden against Damascus cannot be told without Ephraim inside it, because the two were allied against Judah. Both fade like a harvest gathered, and in that day people look to their Maker instead of their altars.
9.question: What alliance have you made for safety that is quietly costing you your Maker?

9.title: The Land of Whirring Wings
9.context: The burdens reach their farthest south, to Cush beyond the rivers of Ethiopia, a tall, smooth-skinned, feared people. God watches quietly like shimmering heat, and in the end their gifts come up to Mount Zion.
9.question: What does God's quiet, unhurried watching teach you about the situations you want Him to fix loudly and now?

10.title: The LORD Rides on a Swift Cloud
10.context: The Egypt burden opens with the arrival Egypt's religion never expected: the LORD on a swift cloud, idols trembling, Egyptians fighting Egyptians, the Nile failing, and counsel dissolving into folly.
10.question: What cloud is God riding into the Egypt you keep consulting for help?

10.title: An Altar in the Heart of Egypt
10.context: The burden performs the book's great reversal and performs it furthest here: an altar to the LORD in Egypt's heart, a pillar at her border, and a God who strikes Egypt and heals her.
10.question: Where do you need to believe that God can plant His own altar in the middle of hostile ground?

10.title: Egypt My People
10.context: Then the verse the whole burden section has driven toward: a highway from Egypt to Assyria, the two great enemies worshiping together, and Israel the third with them in a blessing spoken over all three.
10.question: Whom would God have to call My people for the sentence to scandalize you, and what does that reveal?

10.title: The Sign of the Bare Feet
10.context: The horizon returns to the present tense: for three years Isaiah walks stripped and barefoot as a sign of Egypt and Cush led away captive. The sign is aimed at everyone trusting in Egypt's help.
10.question: What sign is God asking you to be, not just to read, for the people around you?

11.title: Fallen, Fallen Is Babylon
11.context: The last burdens are told from a watchtower. Babylon's banquet ends with a chariot and a cry: fallen, fallen is Babylon, and all her carved images are shattered on the ground.
11.question: What report are you stationed to give faithfully, even if it is the one nobody at the feast wants to hear?

11.title: Watchman, What of the Night?
11.context: Dumah's burden is eleven words of question and a watchman's refusal to answer simply: morning is coming, and also the night. Ask, return, come back and ask again.
11.question: What question do you need to keep bringing back to the watchman instead of settling for a simple answer?

11.title: The Valley of Vision
11.context: The burden against the Valley of Vision is against Jerusalem herself: a city on its rooftops feasting while it is besieged, reservoirs dug, houses demolished, and no look toward the One who planned it long ago.
11.question: When crisis comes, what do you stockpile instead of looking to the God who planned your life long ago?

11.title: The Key of the House of David
11.context: Shebna, the palace steward busy carving his own tomb, is singled out and swapped for Eliakim, on whose shoulder God lays the key of the house of David: what he opens no one can shut.
11.question: Where are you carving a monument to yourself that God intends as someone else's doorway?

11.title: Tyre, the Merchant Princess
11.context: Tyre closes the roll of nations: ships of Tarshish wail for a harbor that is no harbor, the crown-giver's crowns are leveled, and after seventy years her profits are set apart for those who live before the LORD.
11.question: What would it mean for your own earnings to end, like Tyre's, as food and clothing for those before the LORD?

12.title: The Earth Laid Waste
12.context: Chapter twenty-four widens the lens past every border the burdens named, to the earth itself: emptied, twisted, its curse devouring, its joy gone like a city of chaos broken down.
12.question: How does worship change when you admit the whole earth, not just your nation, stands under God's judgment?

12.title: The Gleanings Sing
12.context: But the gleanings sing. From the islands of the sea, voices praise the Righteous One over the desolation, until the host of heaven is punished and the LORD reigns on Mount Zion in glory.
12.question: What song can you sing from inside the gleanings, the little that is left after loss?

12.title: You Have Been a Refuge
12.context: Chapter twenty-five is the song reign answers with, personal in a way ruins are not: O LORD, You are my God. He has been a refuge for the poor and silenced the song of the ruthless like heat in drought.
12.question: Which storm or heat in your life can you already testify God has been a refuge in?

12.title: He Will Swallow Up Death
12.context: What the feast destroys is not a nation but the covering: the shroud over all peoples torn off, death swallowed forever, tears wiped from every face, and Moab's pride trodden down in the same chapter.
12.question: Which tear are you most waiting for God to wipe away with His own hand?

13.title: A City with Salvation for Walls
13.context: Chapter twenty-six opens with a song Judah will sing in that day: a strong city whose walls are salvation itself, and perfect peace promised to the mind stayed on God because it trusts in Him.
13.question: What would keeping your mind stayed on God look like in the situation that most unsettles it?

13.title: They Sought You, and Could Only Whisper
13.context: The confession's depth is its honesty about prayer under discipline: poured out like a whisper, labor that seemed to birth only wind. Then the promise answers: your dead will live, awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust.
13.question: What prayer have you whispered that felt like birthing wind, and what does the promise of verse 19 say over it?

13.title: Leviathan and the Vineyard Restored
13.context: Chapter twenty-seven opens on Leviathan, the gliding serpent, slain by God's hard sword, and then the vineyard song of chapter five is sung again, this time with God as its keeper, watering it every moment.
13.question: Which old song of judgment over your life is God re-singing as a song of keeping?

13.title: Gathered One by One
13.context: The movement ends on the great shofar: Israel, exiled from the Euphrates to the Wadi of Egypt, gathered one by one like grain from the threshing floor, and worshiping on the holy mountain.
13.question: Why do you think God gathers His people one by one rather than all at once, and which one person are you praying for by name?

14.title: The Drunken Garland
14.context: The last movement of the first half opens with a garland, and the garland is drunk: Ephraim's proud crown wilts like an early fig swallowed the moment it is seen. Yet the LORD Himself will be the garland of the remnant.
14.question: What garland of yours is wilting even while you wear it proudly?

14.title: Tables Full of Vomit
14.context: The woe comes home to Jerusalem's clergy in the movement's most disgusting paragraph: priests and prophets reeling at the table of teaching, every table covered, and God's word comes to them as line upon line, a snare to the scoffing ear.
14.question: What basic, repeated line of God's word have you begun to hear as background noise?

14.title: The Cornerstone in Zion
14.context: Against the scoffers' covenant with death, God lays His own foundation: a tested stone, a precious cornerstone, and a measuring line of justice. Whoever believes will not be in haste.
14.question: What covenant have you quietly made with the very thing that is destroying you?

14.title: The Patient Farmer
14.context: The movement ends in a farmyard: a farmer does not plow forever, and his tools fit each seed, because his God instructs him. Beyond it, Ariel is besieged and suddenly relieved, a sealed book is opened to the meek, and Lebanon turns into a garden.
14.question: Where is God's patience with different tools for different seasons asking you to trust His timing?

15.title: Carrying Out a Plan That Is Not Mine
15.context: The fifth woe is addressed to children whose rebellion is an itinerary: down to Egypt for Pharaoh's protection, carrying treasures on donkeys to a people who will shame them. Egypt's help is named Rahab the Do-Nothing.
15.question: What plan are you funding and packing for that God has plainly called not His?

15.title: Write It on a Tablet
15.context: The message is ordered into the archive because its audience has already voted against hearing it: tell us smooth things. The result is a wall bulging before it crashes, and a potter's jar shattered beyond mending.
15.question: What hard word from God have you asked to have smoothed down before you would hear it?

15.title: By Repentance and Rest
15.context: Their counteroffer is cavalry; God's offer is the verse the movement turns on: in repentance and rest you will be saved, in quietness and trust your strength. Refused, and yet the Teacher will hide no more, and the road will have a voice behind it saying, this is the way.
15.question: What horse are you saddling right now instead of resting?

15.title: The Breath of the LORD, a River of Brimstone
15.context: The chapter closes on the other patient: the Name of the LORD comes from afar in burning anger against Assyria, and Topheth's pyre has been prepared for the king since long ago.
15.question: How does knowing that God's anger is real change the comfort of His patience toward you?

16.title: Those Who Go Down to Egypt
16.context: The policy gets its third woe, and the charge is reduced to a gaze: trusting horses and horsemen, never looking to the Holy One of Israel. Yet as a lion over its prey, as birds hovering, the LORD will shield Jerusalem Himself.
16.question: In your current trouble, where exactly is your gaze: on the cavalry or on the LORD?

16.title: A King in Righteousness
16.context: Assyria will fall by a sword not of man, and in the cleared ground a king reigns in righteousness, streams run in the desert of the cleared land, and the effect of righteousness is peace, quietness, and confidence forever.
16.question: What would righteousness actually producing peace look like in one area of your life this month?

16.title: Woe to You, O Destroyer
16.context: The last woe of the section falls on the destroyer himself. Zion prays to the God who will be the stability of her times, and the one who walks righteously is promised bread given and water sure, on high places no army can reach.
16.question: Which of the righteous walker's six descriptions in this chapter is the one your life least matches?

16.title: Your Eyes Will Behold the King
16.context: Zion in the closing vision becomes the anti-Egypt and the anti-Assyria at once: a peaceful pasture, a river city with no warships, the lame taking the plunder, and no resident saying, I am sick, because their sins are forgiven.
16.question: What terror from your past would you most like to meditate on and find it no longer there?

17.title: Come Near, O Nations
17.context: The last movement before the hinge opens with a summons wider than any courtroom yet: all nations called near to hear of the LORD's indignation, His sword filled with blood, a great slaughter in Edom.
17.question: What does it do to your faith that God's judgment is announced publicly, to all nations at once, rather than whispered?

17.title: The Reverse of Creation
17.context: Edom's land undergoes the reverse of creation in detail and at length: streams to pitch, thorns in the palaces, every creature on the list taking its assigned mate, because the mouth of the LORD has commanded it and His book records it.
17.question: Where do you see creation being run backwards in your world, and what steadies you in the God whose book still stands?

17.title: The Desert Will Blossom
17.context: Ten verses answer the uncreation the way dawn answers night: the desert blossoms, weak hands are strengthened, and the God who comes with recompense opens blind eyes and unstops deaf ears.
17.question: Which weak hands or fearful heart near you could your voice strengthen with verse 4 this week?

17.title: The Way of Holiness
17.context: Through the landscape runs the road the book has been grading since chapter eleven: a highway called the Way of Holiness, where no lion prowls, and the ransomed of the LORD return to Zion with everlasting joy.
17.question: What unclean or dangerous thing do you need to trust God to keep off the road He has built for you?

18.title: The Spokesman at the Aqueduct
18.context: The oracles step down into history at the exact spot where they began. In Hezekiah's fourteenth year, Sennacherib's field commander stands at the aqueduct where Isaiah once met Ahaz, and preaches surrender to the men on the wall.
18.question: When a threat starts preaching theology at you, how do you tell its use of God's name from God's own voice?

18.title: On What Are You Trusting?
18.context: His terms are generous and his logic is a roll call of gods who failed: do not let Hezekiah deceive you, do not let your God deceive you. The king's answer is silence, torn clothes, and messengers sent to Isaiah.
18.question: Which collapsed god in the roll call is the enemy using to argue that your God will be next?

18.title: Hezekiah's Prayer in the Temple
18.context: Isaiah's answer comes back at once: do not be afraid. Then the letter arrives, and Hezekiah spreads it before the LORD and prays the prayer that names God's purpose: that all kingdoms may know that You alone are God.
18.question: What letter in your life needs to be spread out before God rather than answered by you?

18.title: The Hook in Your Nose
18.context: The answering oracle dignifies Assyria with an arraignment: the virgin daughter of Zion despises you, your stack of conquered kings proves nothing, and God will put His hook in your nose. That night the angel of the LORD strikes 185,000, and Sennacherib goes home to be murdered by his own sons.
18.question: Where do you need to leave the defense of God's name, and your own, to God Himself?

19.title: Set Your House in Order
19.context: In those days the war comes inside the king's own body: Isaiah brings a death sentence, and Hezekiah turns his face to the wall and weeps and prays. Before Isaiah crosses the courtyard, the word reverses: fifteen years added, and the sun's shadow runs backwards as the sign.
19.question: How would you pray differently if you believed God could answer before the messenger reached the courtyard?

19.title: The Writing of Hezekiah
19.context: Then the chapter does something no other chapter in the book's first half does: it hands the pen to the king. Hezekiah's own writing remembers the terror at noon, the tent folded like a weaver's web, and lands where the book's songs land: the living, the living, they praise You.
19.question: What would your own writing say if you recorded, in your words, what God brought you through?

19.title: The Envoys from Babylon
19.context: What Hezekiah does with the fifteen years brings the ambassadors: letters and a gift from Babylon, and a king who shows them everything, nothing in his palace withheld. Isaiah's oracle names the day when everything shown will be carried to Babylon, and the king calls the word good because there will be peace in his days.
19.question: What are you showing off today that your grandchildren will pay for?

20.title: Comfort, Comfort My People
20.context: Between chapter thirty-nine and chapter forty, roughly a century and a half passes unspoken: the exile has happened, and the book now speaks past it. Double has been received for her sins, and a voice cries in the wilderness to prepare the way of the LORD.
20.question: What comfort from God have you been refusing because the road to it runs through a wilderness?

20.title: All Flesh Is Grass
20.context: A second voice commissions the herald, and the exchange is preserved: cry out; what shall I cry? All flesh is grass, and the grass withers, but the word of our God stands forever. The Victor who arrives then gathers lambs in His arms.
20.question: Which grass in your life, impressive and fading, have you been treating as permanent?

20.title: Who Has Measured the Waters?
20.context: Then the chapter builds its case, and the case is scale: waters measured in a palm, nations as a drop in a bucket, idols as a craftsman's project, and the Holy One lifting the starry host out by number and name.
20.question: What problem have you been measuring against yourself that this chapter measures against the palm of God's hand?

20.title: They Will Mount Up on Wings
20.context: The argument lands on the exiles' own complaint, quoted back to them word for word: my way is hidden. The everlasting God does not grow weary, and those who wait on Him exchange their strength and rise on wings like eagles.
20.question: What does waiting on the LORD, as opposed to waiting for circumstances, look like in your situation?

21.title: The Courtroom at the Ends of the Earth
21.context: The courtroom of the second half assembles in silence from the islands and the ends of the earth. A conqueror is being raised from the east, and the nations answer with frantic idol-making, each man encouraging his neighbor at the forge.
21.question: When the world trembles at a rising power, what is your first move, prayer or forge?

21.title: Fear Not, O Jacob, My Servant
21.context: What is said to the chosen servant is the chapter's beating heart, spoken with his full pedigree attached: seed of Abraham My friend. Do not fear, for I am with you. The worm Jacob will thresh mountains, and pools will open in the desert for the poor who seek water.
21.question: Which of God's reasons not to fear in this passage is the one your heart most resists believing?

21.title: Present Your Case, Says the LORD
21.context: The courtroom resumes, and the trial of the gods is conducted on the only evidence this book accepts: tell us what happened before, or declare what is coming. The idols are weighed and found empty, and the first to say to Zion, behold, is God Himself.
21.question: What evidence would your own gods, the things you actually trust, present in this courtroom?

22.title: Here Is My Servant
22.context: The second half's central figure is introduced the way the courtroom demanded, with evidence: here is My Servant, My Chosen One in whom My soul delights. He will not cry out in the streets, and a bruised reed He will not break.
22.question: Whom has the world bruised around you, and what would it mean to handle them the Servant's way?

22.title: A Covenant and a Light
22.context: The commission is spoken to him directly, in the Creator's credentials: appointed as a covenant for the people and a light to the nations, to open blind eyes and free prisoners from the dungeon. Former things have come to pass; new things are declared before they spring up.
22.question: What new thing is God declaring in your life before there is any visible sign of it?

22.title: I Have Kept Silent, Now I Will Cry Out
22.context: The tempo breaks: a new song is demanded from the ends of the earth, and God describes His own long restraint, holding back like a woman in labor holding her breath. Now He will cry out, and lead His blind servants by a way they have not known.
22.question: Where have you mistaken God's long silence for absence, when it was restraint?

22.title: Plundered and Trapped
22.context: The chapter's last paragraph gives the blind servant's condition its forensic summary: a people plundered and looted, trapped in pits, with no one to say restore. God's fire burned around them, and they did not lay it to heart.
22.question: What has God been teaching you through trouble that you have not yet laid to heart?

23.title: You Are Mine
23.context: But now: the book's most personal address opens with two creations, I created you, I formed you, I have called you by name. Through waters and fire the promise holds, because to this God His people are precious and honored, and He loves them.
23.question: What river are you in right now, and what does it mean that the promise is presence, not exemption?

23.title: You Are My Witnesses
23.context: The courtroom reconvenes and Israel's role in it is formally assigned: you are My witnesses. The blind and deaf people, of all witnesses, testify to a God before whom no god was formed and after whom none will be.
23.question: What have you seen God do that qualifies you, however unlikely a witness, to say it in public?

23.title: Forget the Former Things
23.context: Then this God, introduced by His greatest former thing, orders the former thing forgotten: behold, I am doing a new thing, a way in the wilderness and rivers in the desert, for the people He formed to declare His praise.
23.question: Which former thing, even a glorious one, are you holding so tightly that you cannot perceive the new thing?

23.title: I Blot Out Your Transgressions
23.context: Into the ledger of a people who never called on Him, who wearied Him with their sins, God writes the verse the whole second half exists under: I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions, for My own sake.
23.question: Why do you think God grounds your forgiveness in His own sake rather than in your improvement?

24.title: Listen, O Jacob My Servant
24.context: The address softens before the argument sharpens: fear not, Jeshurun, whom I have chosen. Water on thirsty land, the Spirit poured on offspring, and a people who write on their hands, I am the LORD's.
24.question: What blessing in your life is God asking you to mark openly as His?

24.title: The Idol Factory, Part One
24.context: Against that testimony the chapter sets the longest single scene in the book, a factory tour: ironsmiths fainting at their work, a carpenter stretching his line over a tree God made to grow, for a god that cannot stand without help.
24.question: What have you built with God's own materials that you now bow to instead of Him?

24.title: Half for Lunch, Half a God
24.context: The diagnosis is not cruelty but bewilderment at a closed system: the same log warms the baker and is bowed to as a deliverer, and the eyes that should see it are shut so they cannot. A deluded heart has led him astray, and he does not say, is there a lie in my right hand?
24.question: What is in your right hand, held daily and trusted, that this passage asks you to interrogate?

24.title: Remember These Things, O Jacob
24.context: The closing credential is a résumé read aloud: I am the LORD who made all things, who frustrates the omens of liars and confirms the word of His servant. And then the name lands, spoken of a pagan king not yet born: Cyrus, My shepherd.
24.question: What word of God's servant are you waiting to see Him confirm in your lifetime?

25.title: Cyrus, His Anointed
25.context: This is what the LORD says to Cyrus His anointed, and the sentence contains its own scandal: anointed, the word for Israel's kings and priests, given to a pagan emperor, for Jacob's sake, so that the whole earth may know there is no God besides Him.
25.question: Where has God used someone entirely outside your expectations to do His work for you?

25.title: Turn to Me, All You Ends of the Earth
25.context: The clay is warned about quarreling with the potter, in the movement's sharpest piece of household logic. From the warning the chapter rises to the widest invitation in the book so far: turn to Me and be saved, all you ends of the earth.
25.question: What quarrel with the Potter are you carrying that silences your turning to Him?

25.title: Bel Crouches, Nebo Stoops
25.context: Chapter forty-six opens on the day of Babylon's fall, and the picture is a refugee column of gods: Bel and Nebo loaded onto weary animals as baggage. Against them stands the God who has carried His people since birth and will carry them into old age and gray hairs.
25.question: Which of your gods has to be carried by you, and how does that expose it?

25.title: Remember This and Be Brave
25.context: The closing argument is the courtroom's last exhibit, memory itself: remember the former things of old, for the God who declares the end from the beginning is bringing His righteousness near, and His salvation will not delay.
25.question: What former thing in your own history is God's evidence that His counsel will stand?

26.title: Sit in the Dust, Virgin Daughter
26.context: The taunt song over Babylon is sung to a woman on a throne, and its first line is a change of furniture: sit in the dust, grind meal, remove your veil. She called herself queen forever and showed no mercy, not even to the aged.
26.question: What throne in your life is God telling you to step down from before you are put down?

26.title: I Am, and There Is No Other
26.context: The queen's theology is quoted in her own words, because it is the exact sentence God has been claiming for Himself all book long: I am, and there is no other besides me. Her astrologers and stargazers stand by with their monthly predictions, unable to save even themselves from the flame.
26.question: In what sentence do you most often put yourself where only God belongs?

26.title: The Audit of Names
26.context: Chapter forty-eight turns from the queen to the congregation, and the address is an audit: house of Jacob, who call on the God of Israel but not in truth, whose foreheads are bronze. God refined them in the furnace of affliction, for His own name's sake, and will not give His glory to another.
26.question: What name do you wear, Christian, church member, believer, that this audit would test for truth underneath?

26.title: Leave Babylon with a Shout of Joy
26.context: The chapter closes the movement with the ally and the exit: listen to Me, Jacob, I am He, the First and the Last. Leave Babylon, flee the Chaldeans, declare it to the end of the earth, and hear the book's refrain at the gate: there is no peace for the wicked.
26.question: What Babylon are you still residing in after God has already announced the exodus?

27.title: Listen to Me, O Islands
27.context: The Servant speaks now in his own voice, addressing the whole map: called from the womb, named before birth, his mouth made a sharpened sword. Named Israel, he is given Israel to gather, and judged too small for that task alone: he will be a light to the nations as well.
27.question: What work has God told you was too small a thing compared with what He actually intends through you?

27.title: Inscribed on the Palms of My Hands
27.context: His covenant office from chapter forty-two is reissued with the prison work spelled out: say to the prisoners, come out. Zion answers that she is forsaken, and God answers her with a nursing mother's oath and a wall ever before Him, her name inscribed on His palms.
27.question: When you are sure God has forgotten you, what evidence does this passage place literally in His hands?

27.title: Can the Plunder Be Rescued?
27.context: The nations answer by carrying Zion's children home in their arms, and kings and queens become foster parents. The prey will be taken from the mighty, because God will contend with those who contend with His people, and no divorce certificate or bill of sale for Zion exists anywhere.
27.question: Whom have you written off as plunder no one could rescue, that God says He will contend for?

27.title: The Tongue of the Instructed
27.context: Then the Servant speaks again, in the third of his songs, and his portrait is a student's: an ear wakened morning by morning, a back given to those who struck him, a face set like flint because the Lord GOD helps him. The song ends with a warning to those who light their own fires.
27.question: What fire have you lit for yourself to walk by, instead of trusting God in the dark?

28.title: Listen to Me, You Who Pursue Righteousness
28.context: Listen to Me, the chapter commands, three times running, to one people in three postures: look to the rock you were hewn from, Abraham and Sarah, once one man and now a multitude. Heaven will vanish like smoke; His righteousness will never be abolished.
28.question: When your numbers look small, what does the rock you were hewn from tell you about what God does with one?

28.title: Awake, O Arm of the LORD
28.context: The scale argument of chapter forty returns as prayer: awake, arm of the LORD, as in days of old, when Rahab was cut and the sea dried for the redeemed to cross. And the ransomed will return by the road that prayer describes, with everlasting joy on their heads.
28.question: What past deliverance of God's should your prayers be waking up and quoting back to Him?

28.title: I, Even I, Am He Who Comforts You
28.context: God's reply opens with the comfort formula at full strength, addressed to a people who forgot their Maker by fearing men who die like grass. The cup of staggering is taken from Jerusalem's hand and given to her tormentors instead.
28.question: Whose opinion of you, a mortal who is but grass, currently outweighs the word of your Maker?

28.title: Awake, Awake, O Zion
28.context: Chapter fifty-two calls the awakening for the city herself: shake off the dust, loose the chains from your neck, for you were sold for nothing and will be redeemed without money. On the mountains come the beautiful feet of the messenger, and the departure begins: depart, depart, touch nothing unclean, for the LORD goes before you and behind you.
28.question: What chain on your neck is God calling loosed that you keep adjusting instead of removing?

29.title: Who Has Believed Our Message?
29.context: Who has believed our message? The fourth song of the Servant opens with the report no one credits: a root from dry ground, no beauty to attract, despised and rejected, a man of sorrows. Yet the sorrows were ours, and by His stripes we are healed.
29.question: Which of the song's exchanges, His punishment for your peace, His wounds for your healing, is hardest for you to actually receive?

29.title: Like a Lamb Led to the Slaughter
29.context: His conduct under the laying-on is the silence the earlier songs prepared: oppressed and afflicted, yet opening not His mouth, cut off from the land of the living, assigned a grave with the rich. Out of it God assigns Him a portion among the great, because He bore the sin of many and interceded for the transgressors.
29.question: Where is the Servant's silence under injustice calling you to trust the Father's portion instead of defending yourself?

29.title: Sing, O Barren Woman
29.context: Chapter fifty-four answers the song with a wedding and a building program, addressed to the barren woman of the exile chapters: enlarge your tent, for your Maker is your husband, and though the mountains depart, His loving devotion will not. Her rebuilt walls are set in precious stones, and no weapon formed against her will prosper.
29.question: What tent is God telling you to enlarge before you can see the children who will fill it?

29.title: Come, All You Who Are Thirsty
29.context: Chapter fifty-five opens the market: come to the waters, you without money, buy and eat, free. Seek the LORD while He may be found, let the wicked forsake his way, for God's thoughts are not ours, and His word will not return to Him empty.
29.question: What are you still trying to buy from God that He is offering without money and without price?

30.title: A House of Prayer for All Nations
30.context: The book's last movement opens with ethics dated to the edge of the arrival: maintain justice, for My salvation is near. And the door swings widest here: the foreigner and the eunuch, once excluded by law, are given a name better than sons and daughters in God's house of prayer for all nations.
30.question: Who stands outside your circle that this passage is busy welcoming in?

30.title: Blind Watchmen, Mute Dogs
30.context: Then the beasts are invited to the field the watchmen have abandoned: shepherds who cannot bark, lying down to dream, and greedy for wine while the righteous are taken away and no one understands that they are being spared the evil to come.
30.question: What post have you been given to watch that sleep has quietly taken over?

30.title: The High and Lofty One, with the Lowly
30.context: Idolatry is charged in detail, under every green tree, and then the book's altitude changes in one verse: the One who inhabits eternity dwells also with the contrite and lowly of spirit, to revive them. Peace, peace, to the far and to the near, but no peace for the wicked.
30.question: What high place in your own life most needs the visit of the God who dwells with the lowly?

30.title: The Fast I Have Chosen
30.context: Chapter fifty-eight stages the movement's central confrontation, and it starts with volume: cry aloud, do not hold back. The people fast and ask why God does not see; God answers with the fast He chose, loosing bonds, sharing bread, housing the poor, and promises light breaking like dawn to those who pour themselves out.
30.question: Which act of the chosen fast, loosing, sharing, housing, covering, is yours to do this week?

31.title: The Arm of the LORD Is Not Too Short
31.context: The dark chapter begins by acquitting the machinery: God's arm is not short and His ear is not dull. The blockage is named and itemized: hands stained with blood, lips speaking lies, feet running to evil, and roads where no one who walks them knows peace.
31.question: Which item in this indictment is the one your conscience keeps returning to?

31.title: We Grope Like the Blind
31.context: The confession is itemized as carefully as the indictment: justice far away, light expected and darkness received, transgressions multiplied and known. Into the hopelessness God arms Himself as a warrior, because He saw no intercessor, and promises that the Redeemer will come to Zion.
31.question: Where have you stopped interceding because the situation looked like it had no man to stand in it?

31.title: Arise, Shine
31.context: Chapter sixty is the sunrise the confession was groping for, and it opens with the imperative the whole book has been building toward: arise, shine, for your light has come. Nations walk by it, sons come from afar, and the wealth of the sea is turned toward the city.
31.question: What part of your life is God calling to get up, not because the dark is gone, but because the light has come?

31.title: Your Light Will Never Set
31.context: The city's upgrade is metallurgical and constitutional in the same breath: gold for bronze, peace as her governor, violence heard no more in her land. The sun will never set on her, because the LORD will be her everlasting light, and the least one will become a thousand.
31.question: Which small one in your world, possibly you, needs to hear that God multiplies the least?

32.title: The Spirit of the Lord GOD Is on Me
32.context: The Spirit of the Lord GOD is on Me, because the LORD has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives and the year of the LORD's favor. Ashes are traded for a garland, and the ruined cities are rebuilt by the people once shamed.
32.question: Which item in the Anointed One's commission is the one you most need Him to perform for you?

32.title: Instead of Shame, a Double Portion
32.context: The shame account is settled in the exile's own currency, double: double portion in the land, everlasting joy instead of disgrace. The prophet answers dressed by God Himself, in garments of salvation and a robe of righteousness, like a bride decked with jewels.
32.question: What shame are you still keeping accounts on that God says He has settled at double?

32.title: Watchmen Who Will Never Be Silent
32.context: Chapter sixty-two opens with a vow of insomnia: for Zion's sake I will not be silent, and on her walls watchmen are posted who give God Himself no rest until He makes Jerusalem the praise of the earth.
32.question: What prayer have you retired that this chapter calls you to un-retire and give God no rest over?

32.title: Sworn by His Right Hand
32.context: The oath backing the watchmen is sworn by God's right hand and mighty arm, and its content is a farm bill: your grain will never again feed your enemies. The city is renamed Sought Out, Not Forsaken, and the herald's cry goes to the end of the earth: say to Daughter Zion, see, your Savior comes.
32.question: Which name have you been living under, Forsaken or something like it, that God has already renamed?

33.title: Who Is This Coming from Edom?
33.context: The book's last dialogue opens as a sentry's challenge to a figure approaching from the south, robes splendid and stained red. He trod the winepress alone; of the peoples, no one was with Him, and the day of vengeance was the year of His redeemed.
33.question: What battle have you been waiting for someone to join you in that God reserves for Himself alone?

33.title: I Will Recount the Loving Devotion
33.context: Then the voice changes entirely, and the book's longest act of corporate memory begins: kindness upon kindness recounted from the exodus, the rebellion grieved over in honesty, and the prayer that Israel's Father would look down from heaven and see.
33.question: What act of God's loving devotion in your own history most deserves to be recounted out loud?

33.title: If Only You Would Rend the Heavens
33.context: And the prayer does not stop at praise; it cross-examines: why do You make us stray, why harden our hearts? The confession lands where the book's factory tour began, in the workshop: we are the clay, You are our Potter, and Your cities lie in ruins as the praying runs out.
33.question: What question are you afraid to ask God that this prayer asks Him to His face?

34.title: Here I Am, Here I Am
34.context: God's answer to the great prayer opens with the complaint reversed: the nation that accused Him of hiding learns He was saying here I am to people who were not even asking, all day holding out His hands to a rebellious people who provoke Him to His face.
34.question: Where might God have been saying here I am while you were accusing Him of hiding?

34.title: Behold, My Servants Will Sing
34.context: The other file is closed in the same chapter with the refusal formula the book keeps sentencing: those who forsake the LORD will hunger; My servants will eat, drink, rejoice, and sing. Then the horizon opens beyond everything the book has promised: new heavens and a new earth, no more weeping, and the wolf and the lamb feeding together.
34.question: Which former trouble of yours is God promising will not even be remembered?

34.title: Heaven Is My Throne
34.context: The last chapter opens by downsizing the temple: heaven is My throne and earth My footstool, so what house could you build Me? The person God looks on is the humble and contrite who trembles at His word, and to that trembling Zion, Jerusalem becomes a nursing mother whose children are comforted in her lap.
34.question: What house have you been building for God that He is politely stepping around to reach the humble instead?

34.title: All Flesh Will Come to Worship
34.context: The ending widens and darkens in the same motion: the nations gathered, survivors sent with the good news to coasts that have never heard His name, and as the new heavens and new earth endure, all flesh comes to worship. The book's last sight is the one the retelling does not avert its eyes from, the judgment that makes the worship honest.
34.question: How does ending at this sight change the way you receive everything the book promised before it?
